Short case 13 · General Surgery

Cervical Lymphadenopathy

In India this case is tuberculosis until proved otherwise, and a secondary until proved otherwise, in that order of frequency and the reverse order of urgency. The level of the node tells you where to look for the primary, and that is the examiner's real question.

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework

1The levels, which both books agree on

LevelGroupBoundaries and what it drains
ISubmental (Ia) and submandibular (Ib) Lip, anterior tongue, floor of mouth, cheek
IIUpper jugular / upper deep cervical Base of skull to hyoid; lateral sternohyoid to posterior sternomastoid. IIa is below and in front of the spinal accessory nerve, IIb above and posterior. Contains the jugulodigastric node and drains naso- and oropharynx including tonsil, posterolateral oral cavity, superior larynx and piriform fossa. The commonest site of enlargement.
IIIMiddle jugular Hyoid to omohyoid or cricothyroid membrane
IVLower jugular Omohyoid or cricothyroid membrane to clavicle. Where an abdominal or thoracic primary declares itself on the left
VPosterior triangle, including supraclavicular Posterior border of sternocleidomastoid to anterior border of trapezius
VIAnterior compartment Central: thyroid, including Delphian and paratracheal nodes
VIISuperior mediastinal

SRB ch.5 p.435, which calls it the Memorial Sloan Kettering levelling; B&L ch.52 p.778, which gives the same system and adds that level II nodes are the commonest site of enlargement and the most readily palpated.

Why the level is the first thing you report Because it narrows the primary before any investigation. B&L: the level II nodes "drain the naso- and oropharynx, including the tonsils, posterolateral aspects of the oral cavity and the superior aspects of the larynx and piriform fossae. They are the most common sites of enlargement."B&L 52 · p.778

So: level I sends you to the lip, anterior tongue and floor of mouth; level II to the tonsil, nasopharynx and oropharynx; levels III and IV to the larynx, hypopharynx and thyroid; level IV or V on the left to the stomach, pancreas and lung; level VI to the thyroid. Say the level, then say where you are going to look.

2The differential, and SRB's list is the one to reproduce

SRB's differential diagnosis for neck lymph node enlargement
Tuberculous lymphadenitis · secondaries in lymph nodes · HIV infection · lymphomas · chronic lymphatic leukaemia · non-specific lymphadenitis · infectious mononucleosis · sarcoidosis · actinomycosis · brucellosis · toxoplasmosis.SRB 5 · p.431 The first four carry almost all the cases.
And the consistencies that separate them
Lymphomas are smooth, non-tender, firm, of India-rubber consistency.SRB 5 · p.431 Tuberculous nodes are matted, which is the single most useful sign in this case. Secondaries are hard, discrete at first then fixed. S Das's version for the iliac region applies equally in the neck: "Secondary carcinoma will be felt as a hard, nodular and fixed mass. Primary growth should be looked for and if found settles the diagnosis."Das 35 · p.535
The filarial node, which is an Indian answer
S Das: "Filarial nodes are suspected when the patient suffers from periodic attacks of fever with simultaneous tenderness and swelling of the nodes. Eosinophilia and demonstration of microfilaria in blood drawn at night will clinch the diagnosis."Das 35 · p.535 Blood drawn at night is the detail that gets the mark.
And the lymphosarcoma pattern
S Das: "Lymphosarcoma gives rise to rapid enlargement of the nodes without other complaints in the young subject."Das 35 · p.535 Rapid, painless, young, and otherwise well.

3Tuberculous lymphadenitis, in five stages

SRB's five stages, which is the answer to "how does it progress?" 1. Stage of infection and lymphadenitis.
2. Stage of periadenitis with matting.
3. Stage of caseating necrosis and cold abscess formation.
4. Stage of formation of a collar stud abscess.
5. Stage of formation of a sinus, which discharges.SRB 5 · p.432

Every physical sign in this case belongs to one of those five stages, and naming the stage is more impressive than naming the disease. Matting is stage 2, and it is caused by periadenitis: the capsules of adjacent nodes become inflamed and stick together. SRB's cut specimen shows yellowish caseating material with periadenitis, that is matting.SRB 5 · p.432

And the histology: caseating material with Langhans-type giant cells; the caseating type is more common than the hyperplastic type.SRB 5 · p.432
The collar stud abscess, explained
A cold abscess in a deep node points through the deep fascia into the subcutaneous plane, giving an hourglass or collar-stud shape: a deep collection and a superficial one joined by a narrow neck through the fascia. SRB illustrates exactly this sequence: cold abscess due to caseating tuberculous lymphadenitis, then collar stud abscess, then tuberculous sinus formation after drainage.SRB 5 · p.431
Why it mattersBecause incising it in the wrong place creates stage 5.
How to aspirate a cold abscess, which is examinable
SRB: "'Zig-zag' aspiration by wide bore needle in a non-dependent area to prevent sinus formation." If it must be drained: "Drainage using a non-dependent incision; later closure of the wound without placing a drain."SRB 5 · p.433
Three reasons in one sentenceWide bore because the pus is thick; zig-zag so the needle track does not form a straight channel to the surface; and non-dependent so gravity does not keep it draining. And no drain, because a drain track becomes a sinus.
Investigations and treatment
SRB: FNAC, acid-fast bacilli and culture are useful investigations; differential diagnosis is branchial cyst and lymph cyst; and treatment is antituberculous drugs.SRB 5 · p.433 Surgery is for the abscess, not for the disease.
And do not forget HIV
SRB lists HIV with lymph node involvement alongside tuberculous lymphadenitis and lymphoma,SRB 5 · p.431, p.433 and in India the two travel together. Offer HIV testing.

4Examination

The signs to establish and record
B&L's printed list for a lump in the neck: history; physical signs; size; site; shape; surface; consistency; fixation, deep or superficial; pulsatility; compressibility; transillumination; bruit.B&L 52 · p.805 Run that list and you cannot leave anything out.
Then the three questions specific to nodes
Are they matted? Tuberculosis. Are they hard and fixed? Secondary carcinoma. Are they rubbery and discrete? Lymphoma.SRB 5 · p.431
Then examine all the other node groups, the liver and the spleen
Generalised lymphadenopathy with splenomegaly moves you towards lymphoma, leukaemia or a systemic infection; isolated cervical nodes towards tuberculosis or a head and neck primary.
And then hunt the primary, properly
Inspect and palpate the whole mucosa: lip, buccal mucosa, gingiva, hard and soft palate, anterior two-thirds and base of tongue, floor of mouth, tonsil and posterior pharyngeal wall. B&L notes that gauze aids the examination and that intraoral palpation may be required.B&L 52 · p.778 Then the thyroid, the breast, and the abdomen.
The node that sends you to the abdomen A hard node in the left supraclavicular fossa, that is level IV or V, is Virchow's node, and its presence is Troisier's sign, classically from carcinoma of the stomach but also pancreas, oesophagus, lung and testis. SRB explains the anatomy: the thoracic duct enters the venous system there, so "dissemination of malignant cells through the thoracic duct into this node occurs easily in abdominal malignancy".SRB 20 · p.841 And the history: Troisier reported many abdominal cancers presenting with left supraclavicular node involvement as an external indicator, 40 years after Virchow, so the node is Virchow's and the sign is Troisier's.SRB 20 · p.841 That distinction, node versus sign, is a favourite viva question and you now have the answer.

5Investigations

FNAC or core biopsy for a neck node? SRB 5 uses FNAC throughout; B&L 52 p.781 says core biopsy is preferred for a neck node
SRB
Uses FNAC as the standard investigation throughout the neck chapter, including in tuberculous lymphadenitis, where FNAC, AFB and culture are the useful investigations.SRB 5 · p.433
Bailey & Love 28e
Agrees that needle sampling is "the investigation of choice when attempting to determine the nature of a neck or thyroid mass", and that ultrasound-guided FNAC or core biopsy is now the standard of care in many units around the world, with CT guidance for deep-seated lesions. But it then states a preference: "Core biopsy is the preferred technique in investigating a neck node as immunohistochemistry tests can" be performed on it.B&L 52 · p.781
Not a disagreement about whether to needle the node, but about which needle, and the reason decides it.

Answer: "I would do an ultrasound-guided needle biopsy. For a node I would prefer a core biopsy rather than FNAC, because lymphoma and metastatic carcinoma are both in the differential and immunohistochemistry needs tissue architecture, which cytology cannot give. If the clinical picture is tuberculous I would still send material for acid-fast bacilli and culture as well as cytology, because the organism matters as much as the histology."B&L 52 · p.781SRB 5 · p.433

That answer works in either book's terms, and it makes the right point: FNAC can confirm a carcinoma but cannot subtype a lymphoma.

And the thing not to do: an open excision biopsy of a cervical node as a first step, when a head and neck primary is suspected, because it breaches the node's capsule and compromises a subsequent neck dissection. Find the primary first: panendoscopy with biopsy of the likely sites.
Ultrasound first
B&L: ultrasound is useful in "differentiating solid lesions, for example malignant lymph nodes, from cystic lesions such as a branchial cyst, and is particularly helpful when fine-needle aspiration is needed to establish the diagnosis"; it is also invaluable for salivary gland pathology.B&L 52 · p.780
Needle biopsy, as above
Ultrasound-guided, core where lymphoma is possible, with material for AFB and culture where tuberculosis is possible.
Chest radiograph, and CT of the thorax
For pulmonary tuberculosis, for mediastinal nodes, and for metastases. B&L: "If a head and neck malignancy is suspected, then CT imaging of the thorax should also be performed to detect distant" metastases.B&L 52 · p.780
Search for the occult primary
Panendoscopy with biopsy of the likely sites. B&L's specific pointer: biopsy of the fossa of Rosenmüller "will reveal the site of the primary tumour in patients with a malignant neck lump that shows EBV positivity",B&L 52 · p.784 that is a nasopharyngeal carcinoma. So an EBV-positive node sends you to the nasopharynx.
And the baseline tests
Full blood count with differential, ESR, Mantoux or interferon-gamma release assay, HIV serology, and in India eosinophil count with a night blood film for microfilaria.Das 35 · p.535

6Rapid-fire viva

Give the levels of the cervical nodes.

Level I submental and submandibular, Ia and Ib. Level II upper jugular, from base of skull to hyoid, with IIa below and in front of the spinal accessory nerve and IIb above and posterior. Level III middle jugular, hyoid to omohyoid or cricothyroid membrane. Level IV lower jugular, down to the clavicle. Level V posterior triangle including supraclavicular. Level VI anterior compartment. Level VII superior mediastinal.SRB 5 · p.435B&L 52 · p.778

Which level is commonest, and what does it drain?

Level II, which contains the large jugulodigastric node. It drains the naso- and oropharynx including the tonsils, the posterolateral oral cavity, and the superior larynx and piriform fossae, and is the most common site of enlargement and the most readily palpated.B&L 52 · p.778

Give the differential diagnosis of cervical lymphadenopathy.

Tuberculous lymphadenitis, secondaries in lymph nodes, HIV infection and lymphoma account for most of it; then chronic lymphatic leukaemia, non-specific lymphadenitis, infectious mononucleosis, sarcoidosis, actinomycosis, brucellosis and toxoplasmosis.SRB 5 · p.431 In India add filarial lymphadenitis.Das 35 · p.535

Give the stages of tuberculous lymphadenitis.

Five. Infection and lymphadenitis; periadenitis with matting; caseating necrosis with cold abscess formation; collar stud abscess; and sinus formation.SRB 5 · p.432 Histologically, caseating material with Langhans giant cells, and the caseating type is commoner than the hyperplastic type.

Why are tuberculous nodes matted?

Periadenitis: inflammation extends beyond the node capsule so adjacent nodes become adherent to each other and to surrounding tissue. It is stage 2 of five, and SRB's cut specimen shows the yellowish caseating material with periadenitis, that is matting.SRB 5 · p.432 Matting is the single most useful sign in this case.

What is a collar stud abscess?

A cold abscess in a deep cervical node that points through the deep fascia into the subcutaneous plane, giving an hourglass shape: a deep collection and a superficial one joined by a narrow neck through the fascia. It is stage 4, and the next stage is a sinus after ill-judged drainage.SRB 5 · p.431, p.432

How would you aspirate a cold abscess, and why that way?

Zig-zag aspiration with a wide-bore needle through a non-dependent area, to prevent sinus formation. Wide bore because the pus is thick; zig-zag so the needle track does not become a straight channel to the surface; non-dependent so gravity does not keep it draining. If it must be drained formally, use a non-dependent incision and close the wound later without placing a drain, because a drain track becomes a sinus.SRB 5 · p.433

How do the consistencies differ?

Lymphoma: smooth, non-tender, firm, India-rubber consistency, discrete. Tuberculous: matted, sometimes fluctuant once a cold abscess forms. Secondary carcinoma: hard, nodular, discrete at first and later fixed.SRB 5 · p.431Das 35 · p.535 Acute pyogenic lymphadenitis: tender and warm.

FNAC or core biopsy?

Ultrasound-guided, and for a node prefer core biopsy, because Bailey and Love 28e states core biopsy is the preferred technique for investigating a neck node since immunohistochemistry can be performed on it, and lymphoma cannot be subtyped on cytology alone.B&L 52 · p.781 Where tuberculosis is likely, send material for acid-fast bacilli and culture as well as cytology.SRB 5 · p.433 Avoid an open excision biopsy as a first step when a head and neck primary is suspected, because it compromises a later neck dissection: find the primary first.

A hard node in the left supraclavicular fossa. What is it called and why there?

Virchow's node, and its presence is Troisier's sign. The thoracic duct drains into the venous system at that point, so malignant cells from an abdominal primary disseminate into that node easily. Virchow described the node; Troisier, forty years later, reported many abdominal cancers presenting with left supraclavicular involvement as an external indicator, which is why the node is Virchow's and the sign is Troisier's.SRB 20 · p.841 Classically carcinoma stomach, also pancreas, oesophagus, lung and testis.

A node with periodic fever and tenderness in an endemic area.

Filarial lymphadenitis. S Das: suspect it when the patient has periodic attacks of fever with simultaneous tenderness and swelling of the nodes; eosinophilia and demonstration of microfilaria in blood drawn at night will clinch the diagnosis.Das 35 · p.535 The night blood sample is the detail that matters, because of the nocturnal periodicity of the microfilariae.

Rapidly enlarging painless nodes in an otherwise well young patient.

Lymphoma. S Das: lymphosarcoma gives rapid enlargement of the nodes without other complaints in a young subject.Das 35 · p.535 The nodes are smooth, non-tender, firm with an India-rubber consistency.SRB 5 · p.431 Get a core biopsy, not an FNAC, because the subtype determines the treatment.

The node is EBV positive and you cannot find a primary. Where do you look?

The nasopharynx. Bailey and Love: biopsy of the fossa of Rosenmüller will reveal the site of the primary in patients with a malignant neck lump showing EBV positivity.B&L 52 · p.784 Nasopharyngeal carcinoma also causes nasal obstruction with or without rhinorrhoea in a third of patients and unilateral deafness from Eustachian obstruction with secretory otitis media in about 20%.

What would you examine after the neck?

The whole upper aerodigestive mucosa: lip, buccal mucosa, gingiva, hard and soft palate, anterior tongue and base of tongue, floor of mouth, tonsil and posterior pharyngeal wall, using gauze to aid the examination and palpating intraorally where needed.B&L 52 · p.778 Then the thyroid, the breast, the abdomen, the other node groups, the liver and the spleen. And a chest radiograph, with CT of the thorax if a head and neck malignancy is suspected.B&L 52 · p.780

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page. In the 28th edition of Bailey & Love, the pharynx, larynx and neck are chapter 52. The two books agree closely here, including on the level system; the staging of tuberculous lymphadenitis and the technique of cold abscess aspiration are SRB's, and the preference for core over fine-needle sampling of a node is Bailey & Love's.
